			Comparing headless browsers for AI data: Playwright vs. Puppeteer vs. Selenium

							 Compare Playwright, Puppeteer and Selenium for AI data scraping. See which browser tool handles JS, scaling, detection and proxies best
			
								
						Author Jake Nulty
					
							
					

		
					
	

	


    

        
            
	TL;DR
	
Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium automate headless browser scraping.
All three handle JavaScript-heavy pages without a GUI.
Playwright covers all major browsers with a modern API.
Puppeteer is Chrome-only and fast for simple scraping tasks.
Selenium is mature but slower than the newer tools.
Pair any tool with browser infra platforms to scale.





From training large language models (LLMs) to powering real-time agents, AI systems depend on massive volumes of fresh, structured data pulled from the web. And that level of data collection isn’t feasible by hand. 



Headless browsers help fill that gap by automating the extraction process. Think of them as programmable helpers that load web pages, interact with content and extract data without using a graphical interface. When paired with browser infrastructure platforms like Bright Data, ZenRows, Browserbase or Hyperbrowser, they can scale across thousands of sessions, quietly feeding AI systems the data they need to learn and evolve.



However, not all headless browser tools are built the same. Each tool offers trade-offs in speed, compatibility, detection resistance and scalability that shape how data flows into an AI pipeline. 



This article compares three leading headless browser tools, Selenium, Playwright and Puppeteer, across key tradeoffs to help you choose the right one for your AI workflow.



Playwright, Puppeteer and Selenium at a glance



These three tools power most browser-based automation today, each with its own strengths and tradeoffs depending on your workflow. Here’s how they compare at a high level:

recommendation:
## Project 1: OpenHands
Browser Automation: Playwright (primarily used via its event-driven and browser-use/agent capabilities)
Integration: Built-in agent tools and execution environment (often leveraging tools like `browser-use` or direct Playwright bindings within its sandboxed runtime)
Key Features: Supports multi-modal interactions, stateful navigation, handling dynamic JavaScript content, and executing browser actions (clicks, typing, scrolling) via LLM planning.
Limitations: Can be resource-heavy, prone to flakiness on highly obfuscated anti-bot pages, and requires proper containerization/sandbox setup for secure execution.

## Project 2: SWE-agent
Browser Automation: Native / Custom web-browsing interface (often interfacing through specialized REPL tools or headless browser wrappers depending on the specific agent configuration/version)
Integration: Built-in tool suite designed for software engineering tasks, repository navigation, and web documentation lookup.
Key Features: Highly optimized for interacting with developer documentation, GitHub issues, and web-based API references; integrates tightly with the software development lifecycle (SDLC) terminal environment.
Limitations: Primarily focused on codebases and terminal execution rather than general-purpose web scraping or complex multi-step browser user flows.

## Project 3: Project 3 (General AI Coding Agents with Browser Automation / Custom Frameworks e.g., browser-use / Stagehand integrations)
Browser Automation: Playwright / Puppeteer
Integration: Plugin/Library integration (e.g., dedicated browser automation SDKs integrated into agent tool loops)
Key Features: High-level abstractions for LLMs to control browsers using natural language instructions, automatic DOM element detection, and robust error recovery.
Limitations: Dependent on underlying browser stability, potential latency in DOM parsing, and varying support across different operating systems/headless environments.

## RECOMMENDATION
OpenHands - **Reasoning:** OpenHands provides the most robust, flexible, and actively maintained framework for full-stack AI coding agents requiring browser automation. By integrating deeply with modern headless browser tooling (like Playwright and specialized browser-use agents), it allows agents to reliably navigate web apps, test user interfaces, and pull live documentation with stateful multi-context sessions.
